title: Foods Highest in Zinc: Oysters, Meat, Seafood, Seeds and Beans

seo.title: Foods Highest in Zinc: Ranking and Absorption
seo.meta_description: Oysters dominate the zinc ranking; meat and seafood provide meaningful amounts, while seeds and beans contribute zinc that is less readily absorbed.
seo.search_intent: Compare zinc-rich foods by serving and explain differences in absorption.

excerpt: Oysters are in a different league for zinc: a 3-ounce serving can provide about 28–32 mg. Beef and other seafood provide less, while plant foods such as seeds and beans can contribute too, although phytate generally lowers zinc absorption from plant-based meals.
content_html:
Some nutrient rankings are decided by tiny differences. Zinc is not one of them: oysters sit in a category of their own.

A serving of oysters can provide several times more zinc than a serving of beef. Beef, crab and other seafood form the next practical group, while seeds, beans and nuts contribute plant zinc with more variable absorption.

The gap between oysters and everything else is huge

FoodServingZinc, approx.
Eastern oysters, raw3 oz32 mg
Pacific oysters, cooked3 oz28.2 mg
Roasted beef3 oz3.8 mg
Cooked blue crab3 oz3.2 mg
Pumpkin seeds1 oz~2–3 mg
Cooked chickpeas½ cup~1–1.5 mg

A serving of oysters can provide eight to ten times the zinc in a serving of beef. This is not a ranking created by rounding error.

Beef is less concentrated but more common in many diets

Beef often provides roughly 3–5 mg per 3–3.5 ounces depending on the cut. That is far below oysters, yet beef may be eaten much more frequently and therefore contribute regularly.

Plant zinc is less available when phytate is high

Beans, whole grains, seeds and nuts contain zinc, but they also contain phytate, which can bind minerals and reduce zinc absorption. Looking only at milligrams can therefore overstate how much is available from a particular plant-based meal.

Soaking, fermenting and sprouting can lower phytate in some foods, although the effect depends on the product and process.

Pumpkin seeds are a practical plant source

One ounce provides roughly 2–3 mg of zinc. That does not approach oysters, but it is meaningful in a realistic serving and comes with magnesium, unsaturated fat and protein.

Fortified foods can change any ranking

Some breakfast cereals contain added zinc. The amount varies widely by brand, so the nutrition label is the only useful value; there is no universal zinc number for ‘breakfast cereal.’

The useful rule

Oysters are the obvious concentration leader. For everyday intake, meat, seafood, dairy, seeds, beans and fortified foods can all contribute. In heavily plant-based diets, it is worth remembering that phytate can lower zinc absorption.

How to turn a zinc ranking into an everyday choice

A ranking is most useful when you translate concentration into an actual serving. Oysters can provide a very large amount of zinc in a small portion, while beef, crab, seeds, beans, and fortified foods usually contribute smaller amounts that may be eaten more regularly. For healthy adults, the NIH lists a recommended intake of 11 mg per day for men and 8 mg for women. That makes it easier to see why one oyster meal can cover a day very quickly, whereas plant sources often work as several contributions across meals.

For people who eat little or no animal food, variety matters more than chasing one “best” seed. Beans, chickpeas, pumpkin seeds, whole grains, nuts, and fortified cereals can all contribute zinc, but phytate in plant foods can reduce absorption. Soaking, fermenting, sprouting, and leavening can lower phytate in some foods. That does not make every meal dramatically more absorbable, but it explains why dietary patterns and preparation matter when most zinc comes from plants.

More is not always better. Zinc is essential, but high supplemental intakes can interfere with copper status and cause other problems. Food sources are usually self-limiting because portions are finite; supplements can concentrate much larger doses. If a cereal or nutrition product is fortified, check the Nutrition Facts label before adding a separate zinc supplement, because the fortified food may already contribute a substantial share of the daily value.

The practical comparison therefore depends on the meal. Oysters dominate by concentration, beef and seafood are dense conventional sources, and seeds or legumes are useful plant contributors. Instead of asking only which food wins per 100 grams, ask how often you eat it, what a realistic serving looks like, and whether the rest of your diet already supplies zinc from several places.

One more useful distinction is deficiency risk versus ordinary food optimization. Someone eating a varied diet that includes meat, seafood, dairy, eggs, legumes, nuts, seeds, or fortified grains may already accumulate zinc across the day without ever eating the top-ranked food. People with very restrictive diets, absorption problems, or other medical concerns need individualized advice rather than a food leaderboard. For everyone else, rotating several sources is easier to sustain than building the diet around oysters or a supplement.

Cooking changes water content and therefore the number reported per 100 grams, but it does not create zinc out of nowhere. That is why comparing realistic cooked servings is usually fairer than comparing raw and dry foods side by side. A bowl of chickpeas, an ounce of pumpkin seeds, and a serving of beef all represent different volumes and calorie loads. Use the ranking to identify useful contributors, then return to the serving you would actually put on a plate.

faq.question: What food is highest in zinc?
faq.answer: Oysters are among the most concentrated natural sources and can provide about 28–32 mg in a 3-ounce serving.

faq.question: Do seeds contain zinc?
faq.answer: Yes. Pumpkin seeds provide roughly 2–3 mg per ounce.

faq.question: Is zinc from plants absorbed as well?
faq.answer: Not always. Phytates in beans, whole grains, nuts and seeds can reduce zinc absorption.
